abstract: Humans readily abstract common relations across situations that look entirely different. For example, when reading a map, we align relations between landmarks on a screen with those in the world around us. Relational comparison forms the basis of analogical reasoning. Here, we investigated how recognising same and different relations instantiated by various simple shapes unfolds in the brain over time. We recorded EEG from adults (N = 20) viewing shape pairs presented in a periodic visual oddball paradigm, in which exemplars of one relation occurred at regular intervals within a stream of the other (e.g., same-same-same-different or vice versa). Frequency-domain analysis revealed robust responses at the stimulation rate (2.5 Hz) and the oddball rate (0.625 Hz), providing an implicit neural measure of relational discrimination. Time-resolved decoding showed that same and different could be decoded while holding Sequence Role constant: relation decoding was reliable when both relations served as oddballs, but significantly weaker when they served as standards. Same/different decoding at the oddballs generalised to shapes and colours withheld from classifier training and was not explained by stimulus familiarity. These findings show that the brain implicitly registers same and different relations at an abstract level that generalises across different instantiations of these relations, and that this information is expressed most strongly when a given relation differs from its established context.
